name: Ahiam
title: One of David's thirty mighty warriors
summary: Ahiam was a warrior from King David's time who belonged to the prestigious group known as "the Thirty" – an elite force of selected soldiers in David's army. He is identified as the son of Shachar the Hararite (in 1 Chronicles) or Sharar the Hararite (in 2 Samuel), where variations in his father's name reflect different textual traditions in the Hebrew manuscripts. Although there are no detailed accounts of Ahiam's individual exploits, his place on the lists of heroes testifies to a significant military career serving David during the establishment of the united kingdom of Israel.

keyEvents.title: Mentioned among David's thirty heroes
keyEvents.description: Ahiam, son of Sharar the Hararite, is listed as one of David's thirty mighty warriors in the heroic roster of 2 Samuel. This elite group distinguished itself through bravery and loyalty in service to King David.

keyEvents.title: Listed in the parallel heroic roster of Chronicles
keyEvents.description: In the parallel list of David's mighty men in 1 Chronicles, Ahiam is mentioned as the son of Sakar the Hararite. The form of his father's name differs here from that in 2 Samuel, illustrating the different textual traditions behind the two books.

versions.summary: Ahiam, son of Sakar (also called Sharar), was one of David's thirty mighty warriors. He belonged to the elite group of soldiers known for their bravery and loyalty to King David. He is mentioned in the lists of David's heroes in both 2 Samuel and 1 Chronicles.

This event should either be removed or rephrased to provide unique information.; [minor] The fourth key event ('Service during David's reign') is very general and overlaps with the other events. This event adds little value beyond what is already covered.; [minor] The summary mentions that the father is also called 'Sharar', which is correct (2 Samuel 23:33 uses 'Sharar' while 1 Chronicles 11:35 uses 'Sakar'). footnotes.text: The name of Ahiam's father varies between the biblical sources: In 2 Sam 23:33 he is called "Sharar the Hararite," while 1 Chron 11:35 uses the form "Sachar." Such variations are likely due to different textual traditions and scribal variants in the Hebrew base text, a phenomenon well known from textual critical research on the Old Testament.

"The Thirty" (Hebrew: ha-sheloshim) was an elite group of warriors in David's army. They formed an extended circle around the three chief heroes and probably functioned as a kind of personal guard for the king. The list varies between 2 Sam 23 and 1 Chron 11, which may reflect that the composition of the group changed over time.

The designation "the Hararite" (Hebrew: ha-harari) attached to Ahiam's father can mean "the mountain man" or refer to a person from a specific mountainous region. It may also be understood as a patronymic or place name. The exact meaning is debated among scholars.

David's lists of heroes reflect a military organization known from other ancient cultures in the Middle East, where the king surrounded himself with an elite guard of personally chosen warriors. Similar structures are documented in Egyptian and Mesopotamian sources from the second and first millennia BC.

The name Ahiam (Hebrew: אֲחִיאָם, 'Achiam) can be interpreted as "brother to the mother" or "my uncle" (from 'ach = brother and 'am = people/relative). Such theophoric or kinship-based names were very common in ancient Israel and provide insight into family structures and naming traditions.
